title: Instability of Life and Things Worldly
paragraphs: What follows is the Tolkāppiyam verse detailing the situations of this poignant kāñcittiṇai theme, besides an illustrative verse of mine:

> Peruṅkāñci that speaks of the inevitability of death; > Mutukāñci that indicates the great truths of life > Which men of sage wisdom bring home to the youth; > Maṟakkāñci that shows a warrior > Wounded in his breast in the battle > Tearing open that wound > And dying in utter disdain of life; > Pēykkāñci that refers to > The devils guarding the warrior wounded in battle > There being no kin to tend him;

> Maṉṉaikkāñci that refers to mourning the death of the great one > Enumerating his deeds of virtue and valour; > Vañciṉakkāñci that indicates swearing a vow > That one would fall into such states stated > Were one to fail to accomplish a task chosen; > Toṭākkāñci that shows a loving wife > Guarding her wounded warrior-husband on the battlefield > Against devils laying their hands on him; > Āñcikkāñci that speaks of the wife > Killing herself with the spear > That took her warrior-husband’s life; > Makaṭpāṟkāñci that shows > Refusal by a chieftain of ancient lineage > To give his daughter’s hand in marriage > To another king of comparable valour > That has come to take him on in a war; > The wife of the warrior killed in the battlefield > Nestling up her face and breasts against his head > And seeing her life ended; > These are the ten substrands of kāñci theme, > Which the authority has decreed.

> The bewildering wail of the kin around the warrior > Who met with a glorious end; > The lonely cries of uncontained distress; > Mūtānāntam, the awed expressions of tribute by onlookers, > As they find the wife ending her life > On the death of her husband in action; > Mutapālai, the bitter wail of the lonesome wife > On the death of her husband > As they traversed the killing arid wastes; > Kaiyaṟunilai, the helpless cries of anguish of the kindred folk > At the death of the ones who counted in their lives; > Taputāranilai, the piteous state of the bereaved husband; > Tāpatānilai, the misery of having been bereaved of one’s loving husband;

> Pālai nilai, the words of resentment by the wife, > Who prepares to enter into the funeral pyre of her husband, > At those that tend to weaken her resolve; > Talaippeyalnilai, the supreme act of the mother > That went seeking death on the battlefield > On hearing that her son had a retreat in war; > And kāṭuvāḻttu, the glorification of the graveyard > That perpetually impresses upon the people of this wide world > The impermanence of the lives of men > And its own [graveyard’s] permanence - > These ten substrands of worthy treatment including, > Kāñci theme ramifies into twenty sub-situations. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 24)

> Be it the illumination of the little oil-lamp, > I have provided the expositions of all thematic situations > Included in Akattiṇai and Puṟattiṇai; > Although elucidations detailed of all these situations > I could not give in this study, > Could I afford to leave out Kāñcittiṇai? > Would not kāñci rebuke me albeit gently? > Don’t I know that honeyed heart? > > I am the one > Whose time of the day is split into atoms, > One atom of which is multiplied by a hundred > And is devoted exclusively to kāñci > And spent in all pleasure. > > The kāñci theme unmatched > Is to make a life of eternity > By being reminded of one’s instability of life > Bringing in the analogy of bubbles on water’s surface, > Providing an anchor to the mind vacillating > And standing on renown hill-like.

> Kāñci theme is that > What tells folks > To preserve honour > Be it at the cost of one’s head. > > Kāñci theme tells men > To perform deeds virtuous on the earth > Leaving not a bit of it incomplete > With the realization that > ‘He that lived yesterday > Does exist not today’ > Even when there remains the threat > Of the power of Death around. > > Even if you stand uncared for, > Spirits too will come to your aid > Hailing your efforts large > To make the Tamiḻs flourish. > > Kāñci is routing the wily foe > In the manner of the Pāṇṭiya king > Who swore: “Let me not be the theme of Māṅkuṭi Marutaṉ’s song > If I don’t vanquish the foes and return! > > Kāñci is > That act of the woman > Who bathes with her tears > Her dead husband wounded in war, > Prohibits others from touching her > And stabs herself > With the sword that killed her husband. > > The unmatched kāñci is that > Where a father and mother in the evening of their life > See the suitor for their daughter driven away > With wounds on his back > Who came waging a war for her hand.

> Kāñci is > Where the woman > Clasps her husband’s spear-pierced body > As does a creeper over the banyan trunk. > > Kāñci is > Where the wife leaps lightning-like into the flames > Detesting life beyond her husband > When he remained dead - apart > A sacrifice it is of womankind eye-like > To show that life is no sugar cane > And to hold honour dear as life. > Such is what kāñci is. > > No more energy I am left with > To elaborate further on this kāñci theme; > I stop it therefore at this.
